column3: Near-verbatim account of Iblis refusing Adam's prostration command through arrogance and disbelief.
The immediately following parable of fleeting worldly life frames the deceptive setting in which false allegiance is chosen.
Calls a people fasiq, but it does not clarify Iblis's specific departure from the Lord's command.
Near-verbatim parallel of Iblis refusing to prostrate before Adam.
Immediate continuation denies the misleaders any role in creation or divine support.
Its exclusive resort in the Lord's unchangeable words supports the focus's rejection of substitutes besides Him.
Near-verbatim parallel that names Iblis's refusal of the prostration command.
Contrasts worldly adornment with enduring righteous deeds, qualifying the false exchange named in the focus.
The question about Moses's Lord adds no specific account of rebellion, false alliance, or Iblis.
Retells the command to prostrate and Iblis's exceptional noncompliance.
Immediate continuation shows claimed associates failing to answer their worshippers.
Its generic punishment for fasiq conduct only broadly overlaps the focus's departure from command.
Concise parallel: Iblis is excepted, acts arrogantly, and is among the disbelievers.
The surrounding gathering for judgment supplies a distant consequence setting without clarifying the focus's choice of allies.
A people obeying Pharaoh and becoming fasiq is a broad contrast to obedience to the Lord's command.
Directly condemns taking God's servants as awliya besides Him, the focus's central warning.
The immediate consequence scene shows offenders unable to find an escape from the fire.
The title Lord of the worlds is too general to illuminate the rebellion or false allegiance in the focus.
The Lord's announcement of Adam's creation supplies the narrative background for the commanded prostration.
The immediate presentation before the Lord reinforces accountability in the passage leading into the focus.
It gives a practical criterion for dealing with a fasiq source, though not the focus's Iblis narrative.
Refusal to prostrate when commanded offers a clear, though non-Iblis, parallel of defiant worship.
The immediately preceding record of every deed and the Lord's justice frames Iblis's act and human choice of allegiance.
Its mention of many fasiq descendants is too general to clarify this specific primal rebellion.
Forgetting what was recalled and becoming fasiq links deviation from guidance with punitive consequence.
The surah's closing command forbids associating anyone in worship with the one Lord.
Human ingratitude toward the Lord is a broad moral parallel without the focus's ally or command structure.
Defines jinn and humans as created for God's worship, the direct contrary to Iblis's rebellion.
The immediate continuation identifies the human tendency to dispute despite the Quran's varied clarification.
Explicit signs are rejected only by the fasiq, aligning deviation with refusal of divine guidance.
Responsive jinn who listen to the Quran provide a contrast to Iblis among the jinn who rebelled.
The immediate continuation describes refusal of faith and repentance after guidance has arrived.
God's lack of approval for a fasiq people offers only a general evaluative parallel.
The nearby declaration of truth from the Lord and the belief-disbelief choice extends the focus's warning to its final consequence.
The immediate passage describes disbelievers contesting truth and treating warnings as mockery.
Naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron does not add a distinct neighbour relation.
Directly describes defiance of the Lord's command followed by immediate punishment.
The immediate verse links turning from the Lord's signs and forgetting prior deeds with blocked understanding.
Generic recompense from the Lord does not clarify the focus's themes.
Humans seeking refuge with jinn provides a close warning against misplaced dependence on that realm.
The nearby merciful delay of punishment, followed by an unavoidable appointed term, develops the focus's consequence setting.
Punishment for denying signs through fasiq conduct is a general outcome parallel.
A commanded prostrating entry is not sufficiently connected to Iblis's refusal or false allies.
The nearby destruction of wrongdoing towns supplies the passage's established pattern of appointed consequence.
Naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron adds no specific relation.
Fire and the absence of helpers for wrongdoers are only a broad outcome parallel.
Glorifying the Lord's name does not clarify the focus's particular warning.
Jinn work by the Lord's permission, while one who deviates from His command faces fire.
Turning away from a messenger is described as deviation and fasiq conduct, with hearts then turned away.
Directly commands Israel not to take any trustee besides God.
The parable distinguishes those guided by divine truth from fasiq people led astray through rejection.
Calling a tree a trial for wrongdoers does not clarify the focus's content.
Failure of covenant and widespread fasiq conduct broadly parallels departure from binding divine command.
Exclusive worship of God and the condemnation of association directly oppose taking rivals besides Him.
Return to the Lord is too general to clarify Iblis's rebellion or human choice of allies.
Those punished seek another chance for righteous action after warning, extending the consequence dimension.
The Lord's universal sovereignty is not a sufficiently specific neighbour here.
Forbids reliance on wrongdoers and denies any awliya besides God.
Arrogance and fasiq conduct leading to humiliation in the fire give a broader consequence parallel.
Claimed objects of worship deny the allegiance and identify the worshippers' attachment to jinn.
Unaccepted spending by a fasiq people does not clarify the focus beyond its shared moral label.
Denies wrongdoers any protecting allies besides God or a path once He leaves them astray.
The title Lord of the heavens and earth adds no distinct relation.
Moses rebukes his people for hastening the Lord's command amid their deviation after his absence.
Return to the Lord is too general to provide a useful neighbour relation.
The mention of progeny and wrongdoers does not clarify Iblis's progeny or false alliance.
Faith is made beloved while disbelief, fasiq conduct, and disobedience are made hateful, offering the opposite moral orientation.
Once Abraham recognizes someone as an enemy of God, he dissociates himself, paralleling the focus's warning about an avowed enemy.
Noah's people are called fasiq, but the reference is only generic.
It condemns exchanging what is better for what is inferior and joins that disposition to disobedience.
Changing the commanded word is named fasiq conduct, giving a concrete form of departing from divine command.
Defines mutual awliya among committed believers, supplying a positive framework against the focus's false allegiance.
A divine command followed by fasiq conduct and destruction forms a close consequence pattern.
Its legal use of enemy status does not materially clarify the focus's spiritual enemy and allies.
A plea for increased punishment in the fire does not add a focused relation.
The alternation of hardship and ease does not clarify the focus's themes.
Forgetting God produces self-forgetfulness and identifies people as fasiq, closely illuminating departure from divine orientation.
Joseph's protection from evil through his Lord is a distant contrast to Iblis's chosen rebellion.
Magnifying the Lord establishes the value order directly opposed to Iblis's arrogance.
Denies wrongdoers any awliya besides God and connects that condition to failed hearing and sight.
Moses seeks refuge in his Lord from every arrogant denier of the Day of Account, a moral parallel to Iblis.
Intrigue against the Messenger and God's eventual triumph do not clarify the focus.
The destruction of fasiq people gives a general consequence parallel while patience remains contextual.
Calling wrongdoing after faith fusuq gives only a broad ethical overlap.
Fear of standing before the Lord is too general to clarify the focus's rebellion and false alliance.
Its enemy and righteous-action language belongs to a distinct communal military setting.
Holding the revealed tablets firmly is contrasted with the dwelling of the fasiq, reinforcing obedience to command.
Pharaoh's opposition to Moses's appeal to his Lord supplies a distant command-and-corruption contrast.
The nearby return of a wrongdoer to his Lord for final punishment continues the surah's accountability frame.
Carrying revelation without acting on it broadly resembles failure to honor divine guidance.
Iblis's assembled forces give a direct narrative counterpart to the focus's warning about his progeny and following.
Marked punishment for transgressors does not clarify the focus's specific relation.
Joseph's placement and God's prevailing plan do not provide a useful neighbour relation.
Taking religious authorities as lords besides God closely parallels the focus's condemnation of substituted allegiance.
God's self-sufficiency despite universal disbelief is too general here.
Iblis addresses his Lord to request reprieve, continuing the narrative of his dependent yet rebellious status.
The contrast between worldly enjoyment and final appearance is only a broad contextual parallel.
Reverent fear of the Lord offers a general contrary disposition without a close link.
People profess exclusive devotion in peril yet associate others after rescue, illustrating unstable allegiance.
Invoking another god without proof is condemned and returned to reckoning before the Lord, directly opposing false association.
Satan causes Adam and his wife to slip and lose their place, extending the consequences of the primal rebellion.
Explicitly forbids following Satan's footsteps and identifies him as an open enemy.
The command to enter submission wholly is immediately grounded in the warning not to follow Satan's footsteps.
Satan's promise of poverty and command to indecency illustrates his misleading direction against divine promise and forgiveness.
Mary and her offspring are commended to God's protection from the rejected Satan, directly linking Satan with progeny and refuge.
A setback is attributed to Satan's causing believers to slip through some of their deeds, while God pardons them.
Satan magnifies the fear of his allies, whereas believers are directed to fear God alone.
Those seeking judgment from false authorities are described as targets of Satan's desire to lead them far astray.
Contrasts believers who fight in God's cause with disbelievers who fight in Satan's cause and commands resistance to Satan's allies.
Associating others with God is connected to invoking a rebellious Satan.
Satan is cursed after declaring that he will take an appointed share of God's servants.
Satan's stated program is to mislead, arouse false hopes, and command disfiguring disobedience; obeying him is ruinous substitution.
Satan's promises and hopes are explicitly called deception.
Wine and gambling are named Satan's defiling work and believers are commanded to avoid them.
Satan seeks enmity and diversion from God's remembrance and prayer, making his hostile purpose concrete.
Satan makes rejected people's deeds attractive, explaining persistence in their refusal.
Devils among jinn and humans inspire deceptive speech to one another, expanding the focus's warning beyond Iblis's progeny.
Devils inspire their allies to dispute, and obedience to those allies is equated with association.
After enumerating God's provision, the verse forbids following Satan's footsteps because he is an open enemy.
God questions Iblis's refusal to prostrate; Iblis grounds it in arrogant comparison with Adam.
Iblis is commanded to descend because arrogance has no place there, and he is made abased.
Iblis asks for reprieve until the resurrection, showing continued dependence on the authority he defied.
God grants Iblis the requested reprieve for an appointed period.
Iblis vows to lie in ambush on God's straight path to mislead people.
Iblis describes his assault from every direction to make people ungrateful.
Iblis's expulsion and the filling of Hell with his followers state the outcome of his hostile allegiance.
Satan whispers to Adam and his wife to expose what was hidden from them and entice them with false promises.
Satan reinforces the temptation by swearing falsely that he is a sincere adviser.
Satan's deception causes their fall and makes the loss of their prior state visible.
Believers are warned not to let Satan tempt them as he removed their parents from the garden; he and his tribe see humans from an unseen position.
Satan beautifies the opponents' deeds, promises support, then disavows them when the reality of divine power appears.
Joseph is warned not to tell his vision to his brothers because Satan is an open enemy to humankind.
Satan causes the imprisoned man to forget mentioning Joseph to his lord, illustrating obstruction through forgetfulness.
Joseph attributes the estrangement between himself and his brothers to Satan's causing discord.
On the Day of Judgment Satan disavows his followers, admits only to inviting them, and confirms that no authority compelled their response.
After Adam is formed and given spirit, the angels are commanded to prostrate to him.
All the angels comply with the prostration command.
Iblis alone refuses to be among those who prostrate.
God asks Iblis why he is not among the prostrators, directly exposing his refusal.
Iblis repeats his refusal on the basis of superiority over Adam's material origin.
Iblis is ordered to leave after his refusal.
The curse upon Iblis is fixed until the Day of Judgment.
Iblis asks for reprieve until the resurrection.
God grants the reprieve for a known appointed time.
Iblis vows to make disobedience attractive on earth and to mislead humanity.
Iblis excepts God's sincere servants from the scope of his attempted misguidance.
God identifies the protected course as a straight path binding in relation to Him.
Iblis is denied authority over God's servants except those who choose to follow him into error.
Hell is appointed for Iblis's followers, completing the consequence of chosen following.
Satan's beautification of prior peoples' deeds and his present patronage of disbelievers extend the deception theme.
Reciting the Quran is paired with seeking God's protection from the expelled Satan.
Satan is said to sow discord among people, revealing his active hostile intervention.
Iblis declares his intention to subdue Adam's descendants, directly paralleling the focus's mention of his progeny.
God identifies Hell as the recompense for Iblis and those who follow him.
Iblis is permitted to summon, disturb, and make promises, while those promises are exposed as delusion.
Iblis is denied authority over God's true servants, who have God as sufficient guardian.
Abraham warns his father not to worship Satan, who is disobedient to the Most Merciful.
Persisting with Satan risks punishment and becoming Satan's ally.
Devils are sent against deniers to incite them, showing their role in escalating rejection.
Satan is explicitly called an enemy to Adam and his wife, and obedience to him leads to expulsion from the garden.
Satan whispers a promise of immortality and imperishable dominion, displaying his method of deceptive temptation.
Adam and his wife taste the tree and immediately face the exposure of their nakedness, showing the cost of Satanic deception.
Guidance from God is given after descent, and following it is set against going astray.
Some people dispute about God while following every rebellious Satan.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray by him toward the punishment of the blaze.
Believers are told not to follow Satan's footsteps because he commands indecency and wrongdoing.
A wrongdoer laments that Satan led him away from the Reminder after it came to him.
Satan makes a people's deeds attractive and bars them from God's path, explaining their failure to be guided.
Satan beautifies prior peoples' deeds and turns them from the path despite their discernment.
Following inherited practice instead of revelation is exposed as answering Satan's call to the blazing punishment.
Iblis's assumption is realized when most people follow him, except a group of believers.
Satan is an enemy; believers are commanded to take him as an enemy rather than an ally, nearly restating the focus's warning.
God's covenant with Adam's children forbids worshipping Satan because he is an open enemy.
The command to worship God as the straight path supplies the explicit contrary to worshipping Satan.
The heavens are guarded against every rebellious devil, locating devils as excluded hostile forces.
God announces to the angels His creation of a human from clay, beginning the fuller prostration account.
Once Adam is formed and given spirit, the angels are commanded to prostrate.
All the angels prostrate together.
God confronts Iblis over refusing the being created by His hands and asks whether he has become arrogant.
Iblis explicitly claims superiority over Adam and confirms his arrogance.
Iblis is ordered to leave, expelled and rejected.
The curse upon Iblis is fixed through the Day of Recompense.
God grants Iblis reprieve until the appointed time.
Iblis swears by God's might that he will mislead all but the excepted servants.
Iblis excepts God's chosen sincere servants from his program of misguidance.
God's declaration of truth answers Iblis's challenge and establishes the final judgment.
Hell is declared full of Iblis and all who follow him.
When Satan provokes, the command is to seek refuge in God, the hearing and knowing protector.
Turning away from the Merciful's remembrance results in a devil assigned as a close companion.
Devils turn their companions from the path while those companions suppose themselves guided.
The deceived companion finally recognizes the ruinous distance of that satanic companionship.
Believers are directly warned not to let Satan avert them because he is an open enemy.
Those who turn back after guidance are described as having Satan entice and prolong false hopes for them.
Satan overcomes people and makes them forget God's remembrance; they are named the party of Satan.
Satan tells a human to disbelieve, then disavows him after he does, explicitly exposing false patronage.
Seeks protection from the evil of the retreating whisperer.
The whisperer casts suggestions into human hearts.
The whisperer is identified as arising from both jinn and humans, broadening the focus's adversarial field.
Following what devils propagated in the reign of Solomon illustrates a destructive alternative to revealed guidance.
When a provocation from Satan occurs, the commanded response is to seek refuge in God.
Those mindful of God remember and regain clear sight when touched by a suggestion from Satan.
Satan has no authority over those who believe and place their trust in their Lord.
Satan's authority is limited to those who take him as wali and those who associate others with God.
Adam's forgetfulness and lack of firm resolve provide the immediate human background to Satan's later whispering.
The Prophet is instructed to seek refuge in the Lord from the promptings of devils.
The prayer also seeks refuge from the devils' very presence.
Moses identifies a violent provocation as Satan's work and names him an open, misleading enemy.
